title: Front or rear disc brake pads and rotors
summary: Standard floating-caliper pad and rotor job. Rear calipers with integral parking brakes need the piston wound in, not pushed.
tools: Caliper bolt sockets (often 13-15 mm or Torx/hex)
warnings: Never let the caliper hang by the brake hose
Rear calipers with an integral parking brake: wind the piston in with the cube tool, don't clamp it
Some ABS/electronic parking brake systems need a scan tool to retract. Check before forcing.
steps: Check master cylinder level. If it is full, pull some fluid out so it won't overflow when the pistons go back.
Loosen lugs, raise and support the vehicle on stands, remove the wheel.
Remove the caliper slide bolts; lift the caliper off and hang it with wire or a hook.
Remove the pads and the caliper bracket (two larger bolts on the back of the knuckle).
Remove the rotor. If it is stuck, check for a retaining screw, then hit the hat section, not the friction surface. Penetrant on the hub face helps.
Wire-brush the hub face and the bracket abutments until clean metal. Rust here causes runout and pulsation.
Clean the new rotor's protective coating off with brake cleaner. Install it and hold it with a lug nut.
Install the bracket and torque the bracket bolts to spec (they're high, often 80-150 ft-lb, so look it up).
Clean and grease the slide pins (silicone or synthetic brake grease). Replace the boots if torn.
Install new hardware clips, then the pads. A thin film of brake grease on the backing-plate contact points stops squeal.
Compress the piston slowly with a C-clamp using an old pad, watching the master cylinder.
Install the caliper and torque the slide bolts.
Install the wheel and torque the lugs in a star pattern to spec.
Pump the pedal until firm BEFORE moving the vehicle. Top off fluid.
Bed the pads: several 30-to-5 mph moderate stops, then a few harder ones, without coming to a full stop on hot rotors.
author: Common Manual seed (unsourced, needs citations)
